items.item: UnsafeCell doesn't itself prevent data races; it only makes mutating through a shared reference legal in the type system. Avoiding actual races is still entirely on the programmer, which is exactly why every safe wrapper built on it (Cell, RefCell) adds its own rule to make that safety hold

at.step: The one legal way to mutate through &T

items.item: The failure in the no-cell-type example isn't about aliasing or undefined behavior at all; it's the same ordinary borrow-check error any &self method hits trying to assign a field, with nothing special about interior mutability involved yet

at.step: Mutate through &self, with no cell type at all

items.item: Cell's restriction to copying values in and out isn't a limitation worth working around; it's the reason Cell needs no runtime bookkeeping at all, which is exactly why it should be preferred over RefCell whenever the value is cheap to copy

at.step: Cell copies the whole value, in and out

items.item: RefCell's borrow tracking is a run-time counter, not a lock; it never blocks or waits for anything, it only panics the instant a conflicting borrow is attempted, which is why RefCell is !Sync and specifically unsuitable for coordinating access across threads

at.step: RefCell tracks borrows while the program runs

items.item: A RefCell panic from a conflicting borrow almost always comes from a borrow that outlives the statement it looks like it belongs to — a temporary Ref or RefMut kept alive by being bound to a variable instead of being dropped immediately at the end of an expression

at.step: A shared borrow is still alive — then borrow_mut

items.item: try_borrow and try_borrow_mut exist precisely so that code that cannot tolerate a panic can detect the same conflict and recover instead, trading a hard failure for an explicit Result to handle

items.item: OnceLock's write-once guarantee is itself a form of interior mutability with its own runtime check, just one that only ever needs to succeed a single time rather than being re-validated on every access the way RefCell's is

items.item: LazyLock's closure runs at most once no matter how many threads call it concurrently; it coordinates that first call across threads itself, which is a meaningfully stronger guarantee than a plain OnceLock plus a manually written closure would give for free

items.item: This topic's three strategies (copy a value, track a borrow at run time, or write exactly once) are not competing options for the same job; the right one is decided by whether the inner value is cheap to copy, needs a real reference handed out, or only ever needs to be set up a single time

at.step: Recap: one way in, three ways to mutate safely

items.item: None of Cell, RefCell, OnceCell, or LazyLock make the data behind them safe to share across threads on their own; that is exactly the gap Rc and Arc from the previous topic, combined with these types, still leave open until Mutex or an atomic type actually enters the picture
